title: Customer Relations & Sales
subtitle: Understand what customers need, sell honestly, recover well from complaints and keep buyers coming back.
description: A practical course for women running small businesses in Nigeria and across Africa. You will learn to discover customer needs through active listening, run a clear sales conversation, handle objections and complaints with proven methods, and build repeat customers and referrals using a simple customer list.
outcomes: Discover a customer's real need using open questions and active listening
Run a six-step sales conversation and handle common objections without pressure
Resolve complaints with the LAST method and fix their causes
Sell ethically, with honest claims, clear terms and safe payment checks
Keep a simple customer list and use it to measure repeat customers and plan follow-ups
Build loyalty and referrals with a costed reward and a 90-day plan
audience: Women who sell products or services, in a shop, market stall, from home or on WhatsApp and Instagram, and want more repeat customers.
tools: A smartphone with WhatsApp (the free WhatsApp Business app is recommended)
Optional: Google Sheets app (free with a Google account)
Your bank or mobile money app for confirming payments

modules.title: Understanding Customers: Needs, Listening and Trust
modules.overview: Before you can sell well, you need to understand why people buy and how to find out what each customer really wants. This module covers customer needs, the questions and active listening skills that uncover them, and the basic protections (honest prices, safe payments, private data) that make customers trust you.

lessons.title: Why customers buy, and why they come back
objectives: Explain the difference between a product feature, a benefit and a customer need
Describe the four things most customers weigh before buying: need, value, trust and convenience
Calculate the value of one regular customer over a year
Name the main reasons customers quietly stop buying

blocks.text: Customer relations means how you treat people before, during and after they buy. Sales means helping a person decide to buy something that is right for them. The two belong together. A trader who only pushes sales gets one purchase. A trader who builds relationships gets the same customer back again and again, plus the people that customer recommends.

blocks.name: happy-customer
blocks.alt: A smiling customer holding a shopping bag
blocks.caption: A satisfied customer is the start of repeat sales and referrals.

blocks.text: Features, benefits and needs

Every product has **features**: facts about it. A blender has a 1.5 litre jar and a strong motor. A **benefit** is what the feature does for the person: she can blend pepper for the whole family in one go. A **need** is the real reason she is shopping: perhaps she sells food and grinding pepper at the market takes too long and costs her money. People buy to meet needs. Features only matter when you connect them to that need.

head: Feature (fact)
Benefit (what it does)
Possible need behind it
rows: She wants to look neat at work all day without sweating
Cake is made with real butter
She wants her daughter's birthday to impress the family
Lasts a full day on one charge
Power supply is unreliable where she lives
Her child has dry skin in harmattan

blocks.text: What customers weigh before buying
Most buying decisions, big or small, come down to four questions in the customer's mind, even if she never says them aloud.

blocks.title: What a customer weighs
items: Convenience: easy to buy
Trust: will she deliver?
Value: worth the price
Need: do I want this?
blocks.caption: Need sits at the base: without it, good price and trust will not produce a sale.

items: **Need:** does this solve my problem or satisfy my want right now?
**Value:** is the price fair for what I get, compared with other options I know?
**Trust:** will this seller deliver what she promised, and will she help me if something goes wrong?
**Convenience:** can I buy easily, pay easily, and get it without stress?

blocks.text: Notice that price is only one part of value. Many customers happily pay a little more to a seller they trust, who answers WhatsApp messages quickly and delivers on time. That is why customer relations is not a soft extra. It is part of what the customer is paying for.
The value of a regular customer

blocks.title: Worked example: what one loyal customer is worth
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sells pap (akamu) and moi moi from a stall near a bus stop in Enugu. One office worker, Chika, buys breakfast from her on most working days.
steps: Chika spends about ₦1,200 each visit (approximate price).
She comes about 4 days a week, so about ₦4,800 a week.
Over about 48 working weeks in a year, that is ₦4,800 × 48 = about ₦230,400.
If Chika also brings two colleagues who each spend half as much as she does, that adds about ₦230,400 more.
One badly handled day (cold food, rude reply, wrong change) could lose all of this.
blocks.result: One regular customer, plus the people she brings, can be worth well over ₦400,000 a year to a small stall. Treating each customer as a long-term relationship is simply good business arithmetic.

blocks.text: Why customers stop coming

Most unhappy customers do not argue. They simply stop coming, and you may never know why. Common reasons include feeling ignored or treated rudely, a problem that was not fixed, quality that went down, prices that changed without explanation, slow replies, and a competitor who made buying easier. Each of these is within your control. The rest of this course gives you methods to prevent and repair them.
Needs that are not said aloud

Customers also have feelings attached to buying. A mother buying school sandals wants to feel she is providing well for her child. A man buying a gift for his wife wants to avoid embarrassment. A trader restocking from you wants to be sure she will not lose money. These emotional needs are real. When you notice them and speak to them gently ("These are strong, they will last the whole term"), the customer feels understood, and understanding is what turns a buyer into a regular.

In the Nigerian market, relationships have always mattered. Many traders already have their "customers" who come back for years, and those customers expect a little extra: a fair price without long haggling, a small bonus (the familiar "jara"), first choice of new stock, or patience on a bad day. This course turns those instincts into methods you can use on purpose, including on WhatsApp and Instagram where you may never meet the buyer face to face.

blocks.title: Ask the quiet ones
blocks.text: When a regular customer stops buying, send a short, friendly message: "Good afternoon Ma, we have not seen you in a while. I hope all is well. Was there anything we could have done better?" You will often learn something useful, and many will come back simply because you noticed.

takeaways: People buy to meet needs; features matter only when linked to a benefit and a need
Customers weigh need, value, trust and convenience, not price alone
A single regular customer can be worth a large sum over a year
Unhappy customers usually leave quietly, so watch for who stops coming

activity.title: Map your product from feature to need
steps: Choose one product or service you sell (or plan to sell).
Write three features of it in a notebook.
Next to each feature, write the benefit to the customer.
Next to each benefit, write one real need a customer might have.
Think of one regular customer and estimate what she spends with you in a year.
activity.evidence: A photo of your feature, benefit and need table and your yearly customer value calculation

lessons.title: Finding the real need: questions and active listening
objectives: Use open questions to learn what a customer wants and why
Practise the four habits of active listening: attend, ask, reflect, summarise
Recognise and avoid common listening mistakes
Confirm a customer's need before recommending a product

blocks.text: The fastest way to lose a sale is to start talking about your products before you understand the customer. A woman who walks into a fabric shop asking for "something nice" could be dressing for a wedding, a burial, a job interview or church. Each needs a different answer. Good sellers ask first and talk second.

blocks.name: listening
blocks.alt: A person listening carefully to another person speaking
blocks.caption: Listening well is how you discover the need behind the request.

blocks.text: Open and closed questions

A **closed question** can be answered with yes, no or one word: "Do you want red?" It is useful for confirming details. An **open question** invites the customer to explain: "What is the occasion?" Open questions usually begin with what, how, who, when, or tell me. Use open questions to learn, then closed questions to confirm.

head: Instead of this closed question
Ask this open question
rows: What kind of celebration are you planning?
What budget do you have in mind for this?
What do you like or not like about this style?
Who will be using it, and how often?

blocks.text: Active listening in four habits
**Active listening** means paying full attention to understand the person, not just waiting for your turn to speak. It can be practised in four habits.

blocks.title: Active listening cycle
items: Attend fully
Ask open questions
Reflect what you heard
Summarise and confirm
blocks.caption: Go round the cycle until the customer agrees you have understood her need.

items: **Attend:** put your phone down, face the customer, make friendly eye contact and give small signals that you are following ("Mm", "I see"). On WhatsApp, attending means reading the whole message, including voice notes, before you reply.
**Ask:** use open questions to understand the situation, the reason, the budget and the timing.
**Reflect:** repeat back the key point in your own words, including feelings. "So you have guests coming on Saturday and you are worried the food will not be enough."

**Summarise and confirm:** gather the details and check: "Let me be sure I have it right: jollof rice and chicken for about 40 people, delivered to Ikeja by 1pm on Saturday, budget around ₦150,000. Is that correct?"

blocks.title: Worked example: a tailoring enquiry on WhatsApp
blocks.context: For example, Halima runs a tailoring business in Kaduna. A new customer sends: "Hi, how much for a gown?"
steps: Poor reply: "₦15,000." The customer may compare on price alone and disappear.
Halima instead replies: "Good morning, thank you for contacting us. I would love to help. What is the occasion, and when do you need it?"
Customer: "My sister's traditional wedding, in three weeks. I have the fabric already."
Halima reflects: "Lovely, congratulations to your sister. So you have your fabric and need a gown sewn in time for the wedding." Then asks: "Do you have a style in mind? You can send a picture."

After the picture, Halima summarises: "So: the style in the picture, your own fabric, ready by the 14th for a fitting, collection on the 18th. For this style the sewing charge is ₦18,000. Shall I book your measurement?"
blocks.result: By asking and listening first, Halima understood the deadline, the occasion and the style. Her price came with context, and the customer felt cared for, so price alone was no longer the deciding factor.

blocks.text: Listening mistakes to avoid

items: Interrupting to talk about your product before she finishes.
Assuming you know what she wants because of her age, dress or the last customer.
Correcting her or arguing about how she describes her problem.
Asking several questions in one breath, so she answers only the last one.
Replying to a long voice note with a one-word text that shows you did not listen.

blocks.title: Silence is allowed
blocks.text: After you ask a question, wait. Many sellers fill silence with more talking. A pause of a few seconds gives the customer time to think and often brings out the most important detail.
Four things to learn in every enquiry

A simple way to remember what to ask is to learn four things before you recommend anything: the **situation** (what is happening, who it is for), the **reason** (why now, what problem it solves), the **budget** (what she is comfortable spending), and the **timing** (when she needs it). Ask about budget politely: "So I can show you the best options, what range are you thinking of?" Most customers appreciate this because it saves them from the embarrassment of falling in love with something they cannot afford.

On WhatsApp, where many Nigerian small businesses do most of their selling, listening takes slightly different skills. Read the whole message and any earlier chat. Reply in the language and tone the customer uses, whether English, Pidgin, Yoruba, Hausa or Igbo. If she sends a voice note, listen to all of it, and if you need to reply by text, refer to what she said so she knows you heard it. Avoid sending your full price list as a first reply; ask one or two questions first.

Listening also helps you discover when you should not sell. If what she needs is not something you offer, say so and, if you can, point her to someone who does. That honesty is remembered, and it is one of the strongest builders of trust you have.

takeaways: Ask before you recommend: open questions to learn, closed questions to confirm
Active listening is attend, ask, reflect, summarise
A summary that the customer agrees with is your green light to recommend
Do not assume, interrupt or argue

activity.title: Practise a listening conversation
steps: Write five open questions you could ask a new customer about your product.
Ask a friend or family member to play a customer with a hidden need.
Use the four habits: attend, ask, reflect, summarise.
At the end, ask your partner whether your summary was correct and what you missed.
Write down one listening habit you will improve.
activity.evidence: Your list of five open questions and a short note of what your practice partner said

lessons.title: Trust and safety: honest prices, safe payments, private data
objectives: Display or state prices clearly so customers are never surprised
Confirm payments safely and recognise fake transfer alerts
Handle customer phone numbers and details responsibly
Set clear terms for deposits, delivery and returns before a sale

blocks.text: Customers return to sellers they trust. Trust grows from small, consistent things: prices that do not change mid-conversation, promises that are kept, money that is handled carefully, and personal details that are kept private. This lesson sets the safe foundation for everything else in the course.

blocks.name: mobile-payments
blocks.alt: A person making a payment on a mobile phone
blocks.caption: Most sales now involve phone transfers, so safe payment habits protect both you and your customer.

blocks.text: Clear prices and clear terms

State the full price before the customer commits, including delivery, packaging or extra charges. If prices of your materials rise, tell customers before they order, not after. Write your terms in a short message you can paste: deposit, delivery time, what happens if she cancels, and how returns or corrections work. Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act (FCCPA) 2018 protects consumers from false or misleading representations, so honest, clear information is also the lawful way to sell.

blocks.title: Worked example: a clear terms message for a cake order
blocks.context: For example, Bisi bakes celebration cakes in Ibadan and takes most orders on WhatsApp.
steps: Price: 2-layer 8-inch cake with name inscription, ₦35,000 (approximate, based on current ingredient prices).
Deposit: 50% (₦17,500) to confirm the order, balance on collection or before dispatch.
Order notice: at least 5 days before the event.
Delivery within Ibadan: ₦3,000 to ₦5,000 depending on area, stated before payment.
Changes: design changes accepted up to 3 days before the date. Cancellation after baking starts: deposit not refunded.
blocks.result: The customer knows exactly what she is paying and what to expect. Disputes become rare because the terms were agreed in writing before money moved.

blocks.text: Confirming payments safely

Fake transfer alerts are a common trick. A buyer shows a screenshot, or a text message that looks like a bank alert, and leaves with the goods. Screenshots and SMS can be faked. The only reliable proof is money you can see in your own account. Make it a fixed rule for yourself and anyone who sells for you, so nobody feels embarrassed to check. A genuine customer will understand; you can say politely, "Thank you Ma, let me just confirm on my app, it takes one minute."

blocks.title: Safe payment check
items: Customer says she paid
Open your bank app
Check balance and history
Amount and name match
Release goods
blocks.caption: Never skip the bank app check, however busy or friendly the customer is.

blocks.title: Payment scam warning signs
blocks.text: Be careful when a buyer rushes you, sends a screenshot instead of waiting, claims the network is slow and asks you to release the goods now, overpays and asks for a refund of the difference, or asks you to send money to receive money. Confirm in your bank or POS app before handing over anything. For large orders, a payment link from a provider such as Paystack, or a business account with Moniepoint or Opay, gives you clear records.
Respecting customer data

Each phone number, address and order detail a customer gives you is personal data. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for how personal data is collected and used, and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) oversees it. For a small business, the practical habits are simple:

items: Collect only what you need for the sale and delivery.
Ask before adding someone to your broadcast list or customer list, and remove them if they ask.
Do not share or sell customers' numbers to other traders or groups.
Do not post screenshots of chats or delivery addresses without hiding names and numbers.
Lock your phone with a PIN and keep your customer notebook somewhere safe.

blocks.text: Personal safety when meeting customers

If you deliver or meet buyers in person, meet in busy, public places where possible, tell someone where you are going, and do not carry large amounts of cash. Collect payment by transfer and confirm it before leaving the goods. Your safety matters more than any single sale.
Promises you can keep

Trust is also built or broken by promises. Saying "It will be ready tomorrow" when you know it may take three days wins the order but loses the customer. It is far better to promise a realistic time and deliver early. If something goes wrong, such as a supplier delay, power cuts that stop your work, or a dispatch rider who did not show up, tell the customer before the deadline, not after she has to chase you. A short message like "Good morning Ma, I am sorry, the fabric delivery was delayed, your gown will be ready Thursday instead of Wednesday. Is that still okay for you?" keeps her trust even with bad news.

Finally, keep records. A simple notebook or phone note with each order (name, item, price, deposit paid, balance, date promised) protects you if there is a disagreement and helps you keep every promise. You will build on this record in Module 3, where it becomes your customer list.

takeaways: State full prices and terms in writing before the customer pays
Only money seen in your own bank or POS app is proof of payment
Customer numbers and addresses are personal data: collect little, share nothing, ask before messaging
Plan for your own safety when delivering or meeting buyers

activity.title: Write your trust toolkit
steps: Write a short terms message for your business: price, deposit, delivery, changes and returns.
Save it as a quick reply or note on your phone so you can paste it.
Write your own three-step payment check and stick it where you sell.
Check your phone has a screen lock and decide where your customer records will be kept safely.
activity.evidence: A screenshot or photo of your terms message and your written payment check

quiz.q: A customer says she wants a phone with a big battery because power cuts are frequent in her area. Which part of this is the need?
options: Staying connected during power cuts
The 5,000 mAh battery
The phone's price
The phone's colour
quiz.explain: The battery is a feature. Her need is to stay connected despite unreliable power. Link the feature to that need when you recommend.

quiz.q: Which question is the best opening for a customer who asks for 'something nice to wear'?
options: Do you want red?
What is the occasion you are dressing for?
Is ₦20,000 okay?
Do you like this one?
quiz.explain: An open question about the occasion reveals the real need. Closed questions come later to confirm details.

quiz.q: Kemi buys about ₦2,000 of goods from you 3 times a week. Roughly how much is she worth over 50 weeks?
quiz.explain: ₦2,000 × 3 = ₦6,000 a week; ₦6,000 × 50 = ₦300,000. Regular customers add up quickly.

quiz.q: A buyer shows a transfer screenshot and says the network is slow. What should you do?
options: Release the goods because the screenshot proves it
Ask for a second screenshot
Ask her to send an SMS alert instead
Check your own bank app and release only when the money is there
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS can be faked. Only money visible in your own account is proof.

quiz.q: In active listening, what is the purpose of summarising?
options: To check you have understood correctly before recommending
To end the conversation quickly
To show the customer how much you know
To repeat your price
quiz.explain: A summary the customer agrees with confirms her need. Then your recommendation will fit.

quiz.q: Which is the right way to build a customer broadcast list?
options: Add every number from your market association group
Ask customers if they want updates and remove anyone who asks
Buy a list of numbers from another trader
Add contacts from your phone without telling them
quiz.explain: Ask before you message, and remove people who opt out. Sharing or buying numbers breaks trust and data protection principles.

modules.title: The Sales Conversation and Complaint Recovery
modules.overview: This module gives you a repeatable path for a sales conversation, from greeting to follow-up, and scripts for the moments that decide a sale: objections and closing. It ends with a clear method for handling complaints so that a problem becomes a chance to win the customer's loyalty.

lessons.title: The sales conversation, step by step
objectives: Follow a six-step path for a sales conversation in person or on WhatsApp
Present a recommendation using benefits linked to the customer's need
Offer a small number of clear options instead of a long list
Confirm the order details in writing

blocks.text: Good selling is not about clever talk or pressure. It is a helpful conversation with a clear direction. When you follow the same simple path each time, you stop forgetting important steps, you sound more confident, and customers find it easy to say yes. The path below works for a stall, a shop, a home business or a WhatsApp chat.

blocks.name: business-chat
blocks.alt: Two people having a business conversation
blocks.caption: A sales conversation is a guided chat that moves from greeting to agreement.

blocks.title: The six-step sales conversation
items: Greet warmly
Ask and listen
Recommend with benefits
Answer concerns
Agree the order
Follow up
blocks.caption: Each step prepares the next; skipping the listening step weakens everything after it.

blocks.text: Step 1: Greet warmly

Greet within seconds, use her name if you know it, and be genuinely welcoming. In person, stand up, smile and say good morning or good afternoon. On WhatsApp, reply quickly and politely. If you are busy, a quick "Good afternoon, thank you for your message. I am attending to a customer, I will reply you in 10 minutes" keeps her from moving on to another seller.
Step 2: Ask and listen

Use the skills from Module 1. Learn the situation, reason, budget and timing. Summarise and confirm before moving on. This step usually takes longer than beginners expect, and that is fine. A customer who has explained her situation to you has already invested time in you, and she will often prefer you to a seller who just sent a price.
Step 3: Recommend with benefits

Recommend one product, or at most two or three options, that fit what she told you. Too many choices make people hesitate and leave to "think about it". Use a simple pattern: **because you said... this one... which means...** For example: "Because you said the children are hard on their shoes, I recommend these leather sandals with stitched soles, which means they should last the whole term."

head: Option
What it is
Best for
rows: Basic version at the lowest price
Most customers; balance of price and quality
Special occasions or customers who want the best

blocks.text: Offering good, better and best options lets the customer choose her level without feeling judged. Point out which one most people choose; it helps her decide. Show, do not just tell: let her touch the fabric, taste a sample, or see clear photos and short videos in natural light.
Step 4: Answer concerns

Most customers have a question or worry before buying: price, quality, delivery or trust. These are called objections, and they are normal. They usually mean she is interested. The next lesson gives you a method and scripts for them.
Step 5: Agree the order

When she shows signs of being ready (asking about delivery, colours, or how to pay), help her decide with a simple question: "Shall I prepare the medium size for you?" Then confirm every detail in writing.

blocks.title: Worked example: from enquiry to confirmed order
blocks.context: For example, Aisha sells wholesale and retail foodstuff from her shop in Kano and takes orders from customers across the city on WhatsApp. A customer, Ruth, asks about rice.
steps: Greet: "Good morning Ruth, thank you for reaching out. How can I help today?"
Ask: Aisha learns Ruth runs a small canteen, cooks about 15 kg of rice a week, and cares about rice that does not break or turn sticky.
Recommend: "Because you cook in bulk and want firm grains, I recommend the 25 kg bag of the parboiled brand my other canteen customers use. It lasts you nearly two weeks."

Options: Aisha quotes today's price for the 25 kg bag from her written price list, and the price for two 10 kg bags if Ruth prefers smaller quantities. Rice prices change often, so she always checks her latest supplier price first.

Agree: Ruth picks the 25 kg bag. Aisha sends: "Order: 1 × 25 kg parboiled rice, price as quoted today, delivery to Sabon Gari tomorrow before 10am, ₦1,500 delivery. Please pay to [business account] and I will confirm on my app."
blocks.result: Every step had a purpose. Ruth bought what fit her canteen, the written confirmation prevented confusion, and Aisha now knows Ruth's weekly usage, which makes a follow-up offer easy in two weeks.

blocks.text: Step 6: Follow up

After delivery, send a short check-in within a day or two: "Good afternoon Ruth, I hope the rice arrived well. Is the quality what you wanted?" This takes thirty seconds and catches problems early. It also makes the next sale feel natural. Module 4 covers follow-up and loyalty in more depth.

blocks.title: Save time with quick replies
blocks.text: The WhatsApp Business app lets you save quick replies (typed by pressing / in a chat) for messages you send often: your greeting, your terms, your bank details and your order confirmation template. This keeps your messages consistent and saves typing.

takeaways: Follow the same six steps: greet, ask, recommend, answer concerns, agree, follow up
Recommend one to three options linked to what the customer told you
Use 'because you said... this one... which means...' to connect benefits to needs
Confirm every order in writing and check in after delivery

activity.title: Script your own sales conversation
steps: Choose your best-selling product.
Write one greeting, three open questions and a 'because you said' recommendation.
Create good, better and best options with prices.
Write an order confirmation template and save it as a quick reply or note.
Role-play the full conversation with a friend once.
activity.evidence: Your written script and a screenshot of the saved order confirmation template

lessons.title: Handling objections and closing without pressure
objectives: Use the feel, clarify, respond, check method for objections
Answer the four common objections: price, quality, timing and trust
Recognise buying signals and ask for the order politely
Accept a 'no' gracefully and keep the door open

blocks.text: An objection is any reason a customer gives for not buying yet: "It is too expensive", "Let me think about it", "How do I know it is original?" Many sellers hear an objection as rejection and either give up or start arguing. Both lose the sale. An objection is really a request for more information or reassurance.

blocks.name: conversation
blocks.alt: Two people talking through a question
blocks.caption: Treat objections as questions to be answered calmly, not as arguments to win.

blocks.text: A four-step method for any objection

blocks.title: Handling an objection
items: Acknowledge the concern
Clarify what she means
Respond with facts
Check she is satisfied
blocks.caption: Clarifying first stops you answering the wrong worry.

items: **Acknowledge:** show you understand, without agreeing that the product is bad. "I understand, you want to be sure it is worth the money."
**Clarify:** ask what exactly worries her. "Is it the total price, or are you comparing with another one you saw?"
**Respond:** give a short, honest answer with facts, a sample, a guarantee or an alternative.
**Check:** "Does that answer your concern?" If yes, move towards the order. If not, go round again.

blocks.text: Scripts for common objections

head: Objection
What it often means
A respectful response
rows: She does not yet see the value, or it is above her budget
"I understand. Can I ask what you were expecting to spend? This one costs more because the fabric is thicker and will not fade. If you prefer, this other one is ₦4,000 less and still good quality."
"Of course, take your time. Is there anything you are not sure about that I can explain now?"
"How do I know it is original?"
"Good question. Here is the NAFDAC number on the pack; you can check it. You can also see reviews from my customers on my status."
"No problem. Would you like me to keep one aside with a small deposit, or shall I message you when you are ready?"

blocks.title: Do not answer price with an immediate discount
blocks.text: Dropping your price the moment someone says 'too expensive' teaches customers to always push, and it eats your profit. First clarify and explain value. If you do adjust, change something in return, such as a smaller size, simpler packaging or collecting instead of delivery.
Haggling with respect

Price negotiation is normal in many Nigerian markets. Know your numbers before you start: your cost, your normal price and your lowest acceptable price. Never go below your lowest price just to win the sale; a sale at a loss is not a success. Many experienced traders start a little above their target to leave room, but very high starting prices damage trust, especially with online customers who compare quickly. For regulars, consider a fair fixed "customer price" that saves you both the stress.

blocks.title: Worked example: handling a price objection on WhatsApp
blocks.context: For example, Funmi sells hair extensions online from Port Harcourt. A customer says her 18-inch bundle at ₦45,000 (approximate price) is too costly because she saw one for ₦30,000.
steps: Acknowledge: "I understand, ₦15,000 difference is a lot."
Clarify: "Was the other one the same type, human hair, and the same weight?" The customer is not sure.

Respond: "Mine is 100% human hair, which you can wash, curl and reuse for many months. Many cheaper ones are synthetic blends that tangle quickly. I can send you a short video of the bundle being washed and straightened."
Offer a fair option: "If the budget is tight, my 14-inch in the same quality is ₦36,000."
Check: "Which works better for you?" The customer chooses the 14-inch.
blocks.result: Funmi kept her price honest, educated the customer on the real difference, and offered a cheaper option by changing the product, not by cutting her margin.

blocks.text: Buying signals and closing

**Closing** simply means helping the customer make the decision. Watch for buying signals: she asks about delivery, payment, sizes or colours, says "my sister would like this", or keeps holding the item. When you see these, ask a simple, low-pressure question:

items: Choice close: "Would you like the blue or the green?"
Next-step close: "Shall I send you the account details?"
Summary close: "So that is two packs of the shea butter and one black soap, delivered Friday. Shall I go ahead?"

blocks.text: If the answer is no, accept it warmly: "No problem at all, thank you for checking with me. Can I message you when new stock arrives?" A polite no today often becomes a yes later, and pressure would have closed that door. Avoid tricks such as false deadlines ("only today") when they are not true; you will meet these again in the ethics lesson.

takeaways: Objections are requests for information or reassurance, not rejection
Acknowledge, clarify, respond, check
Answer price objections with value first, and trade something if you adjust the price
Close with a simple question when you see buying signals, and accept 'no' gracefully

activity.title: Build your objection bank
steps: List the four objections you hear most often in your business.
For each, write a response using acknowledge, clarify, respond, check.
Write your cost, normal price and lowest acceptable price for your top three products.
Practise each response aloud until it feels natural.
activity.evidence: Your written objection bank and your price floor table

lessons.title: Handling complaints: the LAST recovery method
objectives: Apply the LAST method: Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank
Choose a fair solution for common complaints
Respond calmly to complaints made in public on social media
Record complaints and fix their causes

blocks.text: Every business gets complaints: a late delivery, a wrong size, a cake that arrived damaged, a product that did not work. The complaint itself is rarely what loses the customer. What decides whether she comes back is how you handle it. Handled well, a complaint can leave a customer more loyal than before, because she has seen that you stand behind what you sell.

blocks.name: active-support
blocks.alt: A support person helping a customer
blocks.caption: A calm, structured response turns an unhappy customer into a loyal one.

blocks.text: The LAST method
LAST is a simple, widely taught customer service method. Its four letters are easy to remember when you are under pressure.

blocks.title: LAST complaint recovery
items: Listen fully
Apologise sincerely
Solve the problem
Thank the customer
blocks.caption: Follow the order: solving before listening usually makes the customer angrier.

items: **Listen:** let her explain fully without interrupting or defending yourself. Take notes. Ask questions to understand exactly what happened: what she ordered, what she received, when, and what she would like now.

**Apologise:** say sorry for her experience, sincerely and without excuses. "I am truly sorry the cake arrived damaged, especially on your son's birthday." An apology is not an admission that she is right about everything; it shows you care about how she feels.

**Solve:** offer a fair fix, or ask her what would make it right, and agree on it. Then do what you promised, quickly. Common fixes are a replacement, a repair or alteration, a partial refund, a full refund, or a credit for her next order.
**Thank:** thank her for telling you. "Thank you for letting me know; it helps me improve." Then follow up after the fix to check she is satisfied.

blocks.text: Choosing a fair solution

head: Complaint
Fair solution options
rows: Wrong size or colour sent (your mistake)
Exchange at your cost, including delivery both ways
Replace or refund; take it up with your dispatch rider separately
Apology plus a small gesture: free delivery next time or a small discount
Refund or replacement; then review your descriptions and photos
Follow your stated return terms; be kind but consistent

blocks.title: Worked example: a damaged delivery
blocks.context: For example, Bisi's cake for a customer, Tola, arrives in Ibadan with the top layer cracked after a rough motorcycle ride. Tola sends an angry voice note and photos an hour before the party.
steps: Listen: Bisi listens to the whole voice note, looks at the photos and asks: "What time does the party start, and do you still want a cake for today?"
Apologise: "Tola, I am so sorry. This is not the cake you paid for, and I know how stressful this is just before the party."

Solve: Bisi has a plain 8-inch cake ready from stock. She offers to decorate it with the name and send it by car within 90 minutes, free, and to refund ₦10,000 of the ₦35,000 for the trouble. Tola agrees.
Thank: after the party Bisi messages: "Thank you for your patience today. I hope the celebration went well."
Fix the cause: Bisi decides to deliver tiered cakes only by car and adds sturdier cake boards.
blocks.result: The party went ahead, Tola saw Bisi take responsibility quickly, and the root cause was removed so the same complaint would not happen again.

blocks.text: Complaints in public

Sometimes a customer complains on your Instagram comments, Facebook page or a WhatsApp group. Do not argue in public or delete a fair complaint. Reply once, calmly and briefly: "I am sorry to hear this, Ma. I have sent you a private message so we can fix it today." Then solve it privately. Other people reading will judge you by your calm reply, not by the complaint.

blocks.title: When the customer is abusive
blocks.text: Listening does not mean accepting insults or threats. Stay polite, say you want to help and will continue when the conversation is respectful, and step away if needed. If you ever feel unsafe, involve someone you trust. Most angry customers calm down once they feel heard.
Keep a complaints log

Write each complaint in your notebook or a sheet: date, customer, what went wrong, what you did, and the cause. Every month, look for patterns. If three customers complain about late delivery from the same rider, the problem is the rider, not bad luck. Fixing causes is how complaints become fewer over time.
Phrases to avoid, and what to say instead

items: Instead of "It is not my fault", say "Let me see how I can fix this for you."
Instead of "You should have checked", say "Thank you for sending the photos, that helps me understand."
Instead of "Calm down", say "I can hear this has really upset you, and I want to make it right."
Instead of "No refunds", explain your terms and the options you can offer within them.
Instead of going silent, reply within the hour, even if only to say you are looking into it.

takeaways: LAST: Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank, in that order
Agree a fair fix, deliver it fast, then follow up
Reply to public complaints once, calmly, and move to private chat
Log every complaint and fix the cause, not just the case

activity.title: Practise LAST and start a complaints log
steps: Recall a real complaint you have received (or imagine a likely one).
Write how you would handle it using each letter of LAST.
Write your standard fair-solution options for your three most likely complaints.
Create a complaints log page with columns: date, customer, problem, action, cause.
activity.evidence: Your written LAST response and a photo of your complaints log page

quiz.q: A customer asks, 'Do you deliver to Lekki, and can I pay by transfer?' What is this?
options: An objection about price
A buying signal; time to help her decide
A complaint
A sign she is not interested
quiz.explain: Questions about delivery and payment usually mean she is ready. Ask a simple closing question like 'Shall I send the account details?'

quiz.q: A customer says 'It's too expensive.' What should you do first?
options: Cut the price by 20%
Tell her other sellers are more expensive
Acknowledge and ask what she was expecting or comparing with
End the conversation
quiz.explain: Acknowledge, then clarify. You need to know the real concern before responding.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the LAST method?
options: Learn, Ask, Sell, Talk
Listen, Argue, Settle, Thank
Look, Apologise, Send, Track
Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank
quiz.explain: Listen first, then apologise, solve and thank.

quiz.q: A customer posts an angry comment on your Instagram about a late order. What is the best response?
options: Reply once calmly, apologise and move the conversation to private messages to fix it
Delete the comment
Argue that the rider was at fault
Ignore it
quiz.explain: A calm public reply shows other customers you care; the fix happens privately.

quiz.q: Why offer good, better and best options instead of your full price list?
options: To confuse the customer
Too many choices make people hesitate; a few clear options make deciding easier
Because cheaper items should be hidden
To always sell the most expensive item
quiz.explain: Two or three relevant options help customers choose without feeling overwhelmed or judged.

quiz.q: Three customers in one month complain about crushed parcels from the same dispatch rider. What should you do?
options: Refund them and change nothing
Blame the customers
Fix each case and also change or retrain the rider, because the cause is repeating
Stop offering delivery
quiz.explain: Your complaints log shows a pattern. Solve each case and remove the cause.

modules.title: Service Standards, Ethics and Your Customer List
modules.overview: Good service must be consistent, not dependent on your mood or how busy the day is. This module helps you set simple service standards, sell ethically within Nigerian consumer protection rules, and keep a simple customer list that shows who buys, how often, and who has gone quiet.

lessons.title: Setting service standards customers can rely on
objectives: Write five service standards for your business
Set realistic response and delivery times and keep them
Use WhatsApp Business tools to keep service consistent
Check your own service using a simple weekly review

blocks.text: A **service standard** is a clear promise about how you treat customers, written down so you (and anyone who helps you) can keep it every day. Without standards, service depends on mood: excellent when you are rested, poor when you are tired or busy. Customers notice the bad days most. Standards make good service your normal.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking items on a checklist
blocks.caption: Written standards turn good intentions into daily habits.

blocks.text: What makes a good standard

A good standard is specific, measurable and realistic. "We give good service" is not a standard, because you cannot check it. "We reply to every WhatsApp enquiry within one hour between 8am and 7pm" is a standard: you can check whether you did it. Choose promises you can keep on your busiest day, not your best day.

head: Area
Vague intention
Clear standard
rows: Reply to every message within 1 hour, 8am to 7pm, Monday to Saturday
Repeat every order back in writing before taking payment
Give a delivery day; message the customer before 10am if it will change
Check every item for damage or expiry before packing
Check in within 2 days of every delivery

blocks.title: Five standards for a small business
items: Reply within one hour
Confirm orders in writing
Warn early about delays
Check items before packing
Follow up within two days
blocks.caption: Start with these five, then adapt them to your own business.

blocks.text: Consistency in small details

Customers remember small, repeated details: the same neat packaging, a thank-you note in the bag, the same polite greeting, prices that match what you posted. Consistency tells a customer she can rely on you without checking every time, and that is exactly what makes her a regular. Write down how you pack, label and present your products so the experience is the same whether you or a helper does it.
Tools that help
The free WhatsApp Business app, separate from ordinary WhatsApp, has tools that support your standards:

items: **Business profile:** your address, opening hours, description and website or catalogue link, so customers know when to expect replies.
**Greeting message:** sent automatically to a new customer or one who has not messaged in a while.
**Away message:** sent automatically outside your opening hours, so nobody feels ignored at night.
**Quick replies:** saved answers to common questions.
**Catalogue:** photos, prices and descriptions of your products that customers can browse.
**Labels:** tags such as New customer, Paid, Delivered, Regular, so you can see where each chat stands.

blocks.title: Worked example: a weekly service check
blocks.context: For example, Grace runs a small skincare shop in Abuja and sells mostly on WhatsApp. Every Saturday evening she spends 20 minutes checking her five standards.
steps: Response: she scrolls her chats for the week. 38 of 42 enquiries got a reply within an hour; 4 were late, all on Wednesday when she went to the market.
Accuracy: one order went out with the wrong size of body butter. It was confirmed in writing, so the mistake happened at packing.
Delivery: two deliveries were delayed; she warned one customer early but forgot the other.
Follow-up: she checked in with 15 of 20 customers after delivery.
Actions: set an away message for market days, add a packing check against the written order, and put a daily follow-up reminder on her phone.
blocks.result: In 20 minutes Grace found three specific weaknesses and a fix for each. Without the weekly check, she would only have felt 'busy', not known what to improve.

blocks.title: Ask customers directly
blocks.text: Every few weeks, ask a few customers one simple question: "On a scale of 1 to 10, how likely are you to recommend us to a friend, and what is one thing we could do better?" Write the answers in your notebook. The suggestions are often more useful than the score.

If someone helps you, such as a sales assistant, a family member or a dispatch rider, share your standards with them in writing and explain why each one matters. Then check gently and praise them when they get it right. Your customers experience your business through everyone who serves them.
Opening hours and boundaries

Standards also protect you. Many small business owners answer messages at midnight and feel exhausted, then serve customers poorly the next day. It is perfectly professional to set opening hours, show them on your profile and use an away message. Customers accept clear boundaries far more easily than unpredictable replies. If you offer something outside your normal hours, such as an urgent same-day order, you can charge a fair extra fee and say so clearly before the customer agrees.

Review your standards every few months. As your business grows, you may be able to promise more, such as faster delivery or longer opening hours. When you cannot keep a standard any longer, change it openly rather than quietly failing it. A smaller promise kept is better than a big promise broken.

takeaways: A service standard is a specific, measurable promise you can keep on a busy day
Five useful standards: response time, written confirmation, early delay warnings, quality checks, follow-up
WhatsApp Business tools (profile, greeting, away messages, quick replies, catalogue, labels) support consistency
A short weekly review shows exactly what to improve

activity.title: Write and test your standards
steps: Write five service standards for your business, using the table as a guide.
If you sell on WhatsApp, set up a business profile, greeting message and away message.
Keep a tally for one week of how often you met each standard.
At the end of the week, write one fix for the weakest standard.
activity.evidence: Your written standards and your one-week tally with the fix you chose

lessons.title: Ethical selling: honest claims, fair prices, consumer rights
objectives: Distinguish persuasive selling from misleading selling
Describe customers' basic rights under Nigerian consumer protection law
Avoid false health, quality and scarcity claims
Apply a simple ethics test before making any sales claim

blocks.text: Ethical selling means helping customers make good decisions with honest information. It is not weak selling. In the long run it is the strongest kind, because customers who trust you return and recommend you. Misleading selling may win one sale, but it creates complaints, refunds, bad reviews and, in serious cases, legal trouble.

blocks.name: agreement
blocks.alt: Two people reaching a fair agreement
blocks.caption: Ethical sales leave both the customer and the seller satisfied with the deal.

blocks.text: Persuading versus misleading

blocks.title: Ethical versus misleading selling
items: Ethical
Misleading
blocks.caption: Persuasion explains true value; misleading tricks the customer into a decision she may regret.

blocks.text: Consumer protection in Nigeria

The **Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act (FCCPA) 2018** is Nigeria's main consumer protection law, and the **Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC)** enforces it and receives consumer complaints. In plain terms, the law expects businesses to give consumers accurate information, to avoid false or misleading claims about goods and services, to supply goods of reasonable quality that match their description, and to deal fairly with customers. For products that are regulated, such as food, drinks, cosmetics and medicines, **NAFDAC** registration rules also apply, and the **Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON)** sets standards for many other products.

blocks.title: This is general guidance
blocks.text: This lesson explains principles, not the full law. If you face a specific legal question, such as a large dispute or a product registration issue, check the official FCCPC or NAFDAC websites or ask a qualified adviser.
Claims to avoid

items: **Health and cure claims:** do not say a cream, tea, soap or supplement cures, treats or prevents a disease (for example "cures eczema" or "cures infertility"). These are medical claims, and products making them fall under strict NAFDAC rules.
**False origin or brand claims:** do not call a product "original", "imported from UK" or by a famous brand name unless you are sure it is true.
**Fake scarcity or deadlines:** "Only 2 left!" or "Price goes up tonight!" when it is not true.
**Edited or borrowed photos:** using someone else's pictures, or heavily filtered ones, so the product looks better than it is.
**Fake reviews:** writing reviews yourself or asking friends to praise products they never used.
**Hidden charges:** adding delivery or packaging fees only after payment.

blocks.title: Worked example: rewriting a misleading post
blocks.context: For example, Comfort makes natural body creams in Benin City. Her first Instagram caption read: "Miracle cream! Cures eczema and removes all dark spots in 3 days. Only 5 jars left, price doubles tomorrow!"
steps: She checks each claim. She has no proof it cures eczema, and a cure claim is a medical claim.
"All dark spots in 3 days" is an exaggeration she cannot guarantee.
She actually has 40 jars, and the price is not changing.

She rewrites: "Rich shea and cocoa butter cream for dry skin. Customers like how soft their skin feels in harmattan. 250 g jar, ₦6,500 (approximate). Delivery in Benin City ₦1,500. Patch test first if you have sensitive skin."
She adds a real photo of the jar and a real customer comment shared with permission.
blocks.result: The new post is honest, specific and still attractive. It describes true benefits, sets fair expectations and avoids medical claims that could cause harm or regulatory trouble.

blocks.text: Fair pricing and fair treatment

Ethical selling also means treating customers fairly. Charge the same posted price to everyone for the same item, or be open about what changes it (quantity, delivery distance). Do not take advantage of someone who seems desperate or who does not understand the product well. Do not push a more expensive item that does not fit her need. Keep your word on refunds and returns according to the terms you stated.
Honest reviews and testimonials

Reviews from real customers are powerful because other buyers trust them more than your own words. Collect them honestly: ask satisfied customers if they would share a short comment, and ask permission before you post their message or photo. Hide their phone number and, if they prefer, their name. Never edit a review to say something the customer did not say, and do not hide every negative comment. A page with only perfect praise can look less believable than one that shows a calm, helpful reply to a problem.

Be honest about yourself too. If you resell products rather than make them, do not claim they are handmade by you. If a product is a cheaper alternative to a famous brand, describe it by its own name and qualities. Customers forgive a lower price point far more readily than they forgive feeling deceived.
A quick ethics test

items: **Is it true?** Can you prove every claim you make?
**Is it fair?** Would you be happy if a seller treated your mother this way?
**Would you say it in public?** If this message were shown to your whole church or market association, would you be comfortable?
**Will she still be happy next month?** A good sale leaves the customer satisfied after using the product, not just at the moment she pays.

takeaways: Ethical selling explains true value; misleading selling tricks people
The FCCPA 2018 expects accurate information, honest claims and fair dealing; FCCPC enforces it
Never make cure or treatment claims; NAFDAC rules apply to regulated products
Use the four-question test: true, fair, public, happy next month

activity.title: Audit your sales messages
steps: Collect five of your recent captions, status posts or sales messages.
Check each one against the list of claims to avoid.
Rewrite any message that fails the four-question ethics test.
Write a short line you will add to posts where it applies, such as a patch test or care instruction.
activity.evidence: Before-and-after screenshots or notes of at least two rewritten messages

lessons.title: Keeping a simple customer list and tracking repeat sales
objectives: Set up a customer list in a notebook, Google Sheets or WhatsApp labels
Record the right details for each customer and each sale
Calculate simple measures: repeat customers, average order and quiet customers
Use the list to plan follow-up messages

blocks.text: Your memory is not a reliable customer list. Once you have more than a few dozen customers, you will forget who bought what, when, and who you promised to call back. A simple written customer list, sometimes called a CRM (customer relationship management) record, solves this. It does not need special software. A notebook, a free spreadsheet or WhatsApp labels can all work.

blocks.name: personal-notebook
blocks.alt: A person writing in a notebook
blocks.caption: A simple notebook or sheet can be a powerful customer list.

blocks.text: What to record

head: Column
Example
Why it helps
rows: Follow up and send offers she agreed to
Know which channels and customers bring business
Know when she will run out
See who your best customers are

blocks.text: You do not need every column on day one. Start with name, phone, date, items and amount, then add notes and follow-up dates as the habit grows. The notes column is where personal service lives: her children's names if she mentioned them, the size she wears, whether she likes delivery in the morning, the fact that she does not eat pork. Reading the note before you reply makes a customer feel remembered, even when you serve hundreds of people.

blocks.title: Protect the list
blocks.text: Your customer list contains personal data. Keep it private, lock your phone and any spreadsheet account, and never share it. Only send marketing messages to people who agreed to receive them, and remove anyone who asks.
Three ways to keep it

items: **Notebook:** cheapest and needs no data. Use one page per customer, or one line per sale with the columns above.
**Google Sheets:** free with a Google account and works on a phone. You can sort by date or amount and add simple totals.
**WhatsApp Business labels:** tag chats as New, Regular, Paid, Delivered or Follow up. Good for daily work, but add a notebook or sheet for amounts and dates.

blocks.text: Setting up a simple Google Sheet

items: Open the Google Sheets app (free) and create a new blank sheet named "Customers".
Type the column headings in row 1: Name, Phone, Area, Source, Date, Items, Amount, Notes, Next follow-up.
Add one row for every sale. Repeat customers will appear on several rows; that is fine.
At the bottom of the Amount column, type =SUM(G2:G100) to see total sales (G is the Amount column in this layout).
Use Data, then Sort range, to sort by Date or Next follow-up when you plan your week.

blocks.text: If data is expensive for you, Google Sheets can also be made available offline on your phone, or you can keep the notebook during the day and copy entries to the sheet once a week on Wi-Fi.
Simple measures that guide you

blocks.title: Monthly customer list routine
items: Record every sale daily
Mark follow-ups weekly
Count repeat customers monthly
Message quiet customers monthly
blocks.caption: A few minutes a day and a short monthly review keep the list useful.

blocks.text: Once a month, count three things. **Repeat customers:** how many customers this month had bought from you before. **Average order:** total sales divided by number of orders. **Quiet customers:** regulars who have not bought in a longer time than usual. These numbers tell you whether your customer relations work is succeeding.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a month of customer records
blocks.context: For example, Ada sells shea butter, black soap and body oils from home in Lagos and keeps a Google Sheet.
steps: In March she recorded 30 orders worth a total of ₦285,000.
Of the 22 different customers who bought, 14 had bought before. Repeat customers = 14 of 22, about 64%.
4 customers were referred by existing customers; she writes thank-you messages to the people who referred them.
She sorts by last purchase date and finds 6 regulars who have not bought in over 8 weeks. She sends each a personal check-in.
blocks.result: Ada now knows most of her customers return, that referrals are working, and exactly which six people need attention. Two of the six reorder within the week.

blocks.text: The aim is not perfect records. It is a habit that lets you serve people personally, remember their preferences, and notice early when someone is drifting away. In Module 4 you will use your list to plan follow-ups, loyalty rewards and referrals.

takeaways: A customer list can be a notebook, a Google Sheet or WhatsApp labels plus a record of sales
Record name, phone with permission, items, amount, preferences and next follow-up date
Monthly measures: repeat customers, average order and quiet customers
Protect the list: it is personal data

steps: Choose your format: notebook, Google Sheets or WhatsApp labels plus a notebook.
Create the columns from the table in this lesson.
Add at least 10 recent customers from memory, chats and receipts.

quiz.q: Which of these is a clear service standard?
options: We give excellent service
We try our best
We reply to every enquiry within one hour, 8am to 7pm, Monday to Saturday
Customers are always happy with us
quiz.explain: A standard is specific and measurable, so you can check whether you kept it.

quiz.q: Comfort wants to post that her cream 'cures eczema'. What should she do?
options: Post it if customers say it helped
Post it with a small disclaimer
Say 'may cure' instead
Remove the cure claim and describe true benefits such as moisturising dry skin
quiz.explain: Cure or treatment claims are medical claims. Describe honest cosmetic benefits instead.

quiz.q: In April you made 40 orders worth ₦320,000. What was your average order?
Which agency enforces Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018?
options: CAC
FCCPC
SON
NDPC
quiz.explain: The FCCPC enforces the FCCPA and handles consumer complaints. CAC registers businesses, SON sets standards and NDPC oversees data protection.

quiz.q: Your list shows a regular who bought every month has not bought for 10 weeks. What is the best action?
options: Remove her from the list
Add her to a group without asking
Send a personal, friendly check-in asking how she is and if anything could be better
Wait until she comes back
quiz.explain: Quiet customers need attention. A personal message often brings them back and reveals any problem.

quiz.q: Which statement about 'Only 2 left, price doubles tonight!' is correct?
options: It is fine because everyone does it
It is always required to create urgency
It is fine on WhatsApp but not Instagram
It is ethical only if it is true
quiz.explain: Scarcity and deadlines are misleading when false. Only state them when they are true.

modules.title: Loyalty, Referrals and Your 90-Day Customer Plan
modules.overview: The final module turns one-time buyers into regulars and regulars into people who recommend you. You will plan follow-ups and simple loyalty rewards, ask for referrals in a respectful way, document your real customer interactions for the capstone, and leave with a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Turning buyers into regulars: follow-up and loyalty
objectives: Plan a follow-up sequence after each sale
Time reorder reminders using how long a product lasts
Design a simple, affordable loyalty reward
Begin documenting real customer interactions for your capstone

blocks.text: Most of the hard work in sales happens before the first purchase: getting noticed, answering questions, building trust. Once a customer has bought and been happy, selling to her again is much easier. Yet many small businesses never contact a customer again after delivery. A simple follow-up habit is one of the most valuable things you can build.

blocks.name: message-sent
blocks.alt: A person sending a message from a phone
blocks.caption: A short, well-timed message keeps you in a customer's mind until she needs you again.

blocks.text: A follow-up sequence

blocks.title: Follow-up after a sale
items: Day 0: thank you
Day 2: check satisfaction
Before she runs out: reminder
Special dates: greeting
blocks.caption: Each message has a purpose; none of them is a hard sales push.

items: **Day 0, thank you:** "Thank you for your order, Ada. It was a pleasure serving you."
**Day 2, satisfaction check:** "I hope the shea butter is working well for you. Any questions on how to use it?" This catches problems early, when they are easy to fix.
**Reorder reminder:** time it for just before she is likely to run out. "Good morning Ada, your last jar was about 6 weeks ago, so you may be running low. Shall I set one aside for you?"
**Relationship touch:** occasional greetings on festive days or a birthday if she shared it. Keep these personal and brief, without a sales pitch.

blocks.text: Timing reorders

To time reorder reminders, estimate how long your product lasts for a typical customer. Ask customers how long it lasted them and note it. Then record the next follow-up date in your customer list from Module 3.

head: Product (example)
Typical use
Reminder timing
rows: Ask customers; then remind a week before the usual run-out
25 kg bag of rice for a canteen
Liquid soap 5 litres for a household
Ask at first sale; set the date accordingly
Style kept for a few weeks
Message as the style is due to be taken down

blocks.text: Simple loyalty rewards
A loyalty reward thanks regular customers and gives them a reason to keep choosing you. It should be simple, affordable for you, and clearly explained. Work out the cost before you offer it.

items: **Stamp card:** buy 5, get a small free item or discount on the 6th. Paper cards work, or track it in your customer list.
**Regular customer price:** a fair, stable price for customers who buy often.
**First access:** regulars see new stock or limited items before you post publicly.
**Small surprise:** a free sample or extra (jara) now and then, with a handwritten thank-you note.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing a stamp card
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sells breakfast at her Enugu stall. Her average order is about ₦1,200, and her cost for one serving is about ₦700 (approximate figures).
steps: She considers: buy 9 breakfasts, get the 10th free.
Sales from 9 paid breakfasts: 9 × ₦1,200 = ₦10,800. Cost of 10 breakfasts: 10 × ₦700 = ₦7,000.
Profit over the 10 breakfasts: ₦10,800 − ₦7,000 = ₦3,800, compared with ₦5,000 profit for 10 paid ones (10 × ₦500).
So each completed card costs her about ₦1,200 of profit, about 11% of the ₦10,800 that customer spent.
She decides it is worth it if the card makes customers choose her stall over the one across the road, and she will review it after 2 months by counting how many cards are active.
blocks.result: Ngozi knows exactly what the reward costs and how she will judge whether it works, instead of guessing.

blocks.title: Do not overdo messages
blocks.text: Too many promotional messages make customers mute or block you. Keep broadcast messages to a sensible frequency, make each one useful, and never add people to groups without asking. On WhatsApp Business, broadcast list messages are only delivered to people who have saved your number, which is another reason to earn permission.
Start your capstone evidence now

Your capstone asks you to document two or three real customer interactions and your follow-up. Start this week. For each interaction, keep: the customer's first name only (or a code like Customer A), what she needed, how you used the sales conversation steps, the outcome, and the follow-up you did afterwards with any reply. Screenshots are useful, but hide phone numbers and ask permission before sharing a customer's words with anyone.

Choose a mix: one sale that went smoothly, one with an objection, and if possible one complaint you handled with LAST. Real interactions, including imperfect ones, show your learning better than a perfect made-up story. Write a short reflection after each one: what went well, and what you would do differently.

takeaways: Follow up after every sale: thank you, satisfaction check, reorder reminder, occasional greeting
Time reminders by how long the product actually lasts customers
Cost any loyalty reward before offering it and review whether it works
Start recording real interactions for your capstone now

activity.title: Set up follow-ups and a loyalty offer
steps: Write your four follow-up messages and save them as quick replies or notes.
Add a next follow-up date for every customer on your list.
Design one loyalty reward and calculate its cost using the stamp card method.
Document your first real customer interaction for the capstone.

lessons.title: Earning referrals and communicating your value
objectives: Ask satisfied customers for referrals at the right moment
Write a short, honest description of what makes your business worth choosing
Collect and share testimonials with permission
Design a fair referral thank-you

blocks.text: A **referral** is when an existing customer recommends you to someone else. Referred customers arrive already trusting you a little, because someone they know vouched for you. In Nigerian communities, where people ask friends, family, church and market groups before they buy, word of mouth has always been a key way small businesses grow. The good news is that you can encourage it on purpose, honestly.

blocks.name: referral
blocks.alt: One person recommending a business to another
blocks.caption: Happy customers who recommend you are your most trusted salespeople.

blocks.text: Your value statement

Before customers can recommend you, they need a simple way to describe you. A **value statement** is one or two sentences saying who you serve, what you offer, and what makes you different. Customers repeat it to friends; you use it on your WhatsApp profile, Instagram bio and when you introduce yourself.

head: Part
Question
Example for a tailor
rows: Ready on the date promised, with one free adjustment

blocks.text: Put together: "I sew well-fitted native and corporate outfits for busy working women in Kaduna, ready on the date promised, with one free adjustment." Make sure every part is true and something you deliver every time. A value statement you cannot keep is worse than none.
When and how to ask for a referral

blocks.title: The referral moment
items: Customer is clearly happy
Thank her sincerely
Ask a specific question
Make sharing easy
Thank the referrer
blocks.caption: Ask when satisfaction is highest, and make it easy to say yes.

blocks.text: The best time to ask is right after a customer expresses satisfaction: she sends a thank-you, praises the product, or reorders. Make your request specific. "If you know anyone who needs a cake for a celebration, I would be grateful if you shared my number" works better than "Please tell people about me". Then make it easy: send a short message she can forward, with your value statement, a photo and how to order.

blocks.title: Worked example: a referral request after praise
blocks.context: For example, Halima's customer sends a photo from her sister's wedding: "Everybody asked who sewed my gown!"
steps: Halima thanks her: "You looked beautiful! Thank you so much for sending this, it made my day."
She asks permission: "May I share this photo on my status? I can hide your face if you prefer."
She asks for a referral: "If any of the ladies who asked would like an outfit, I would be happy to help. Here is a short message you can forward."
Forwardable message: "Halima Stitches, Kaduna: well-fitted native and corporate outfits, ready on the date promised. WhatsApp: (her business number). Send a style picture to get a price."
When a new customer mentions the referrer, Halima sends the referrer a thank-you and a small discount on her next order.
blocks.result: Halima turned a happy moment into a testimonial (with permission) and a referral, and thanked the referrer so she is glad to recommend again.

blocks.text: Where referrals come from

Look at the "How she found you" column in your customer list. It shows which customers and which places bring you new business. Many small businesses find that a few loyal customers bring most of their referrals. Treat those people especially well: thank them personally, give them first access to new stock, and keep them informed. Also notice community connections such as a church group, an office, a school parents' WhatsApp group or a market association. Where you are welcome, a respectful introduction or a sample at a meeting can start a chain of recommendations. Always follow the group's rules; posting adverts in groups without permission annoys people and damages your name.

Referrals also depend on how you treat the new customer. She arrives with the expectation her friend gave her. Serve her as well as you served the referrer, and mention the connection warmly ("Ada told me you were looking for unscented shea butter"). If she has a poor experience, you can lose both her and the referrer's confidence.
Referral thank-yous

A thank-you for referrals can be a discount on the referrer's next order, a small free item, or simply a warm personal message. Keep it modest and honest. Be careful with schemes that pay people to recruit others who then recruit more; schemes built mainly on recruitment rather than real sales to real customers can be pyramid schemes, which harm the people who join late. Your thank-you should reward genuine customers who bought what they needed.
Testimonials with permission

items: Ask permission before posting any customer message, photo or voice note.
Hide phone numbers and, if they prefer, names and faces.
Use the customer's real words; do not edit their meaning.
Prefer specific testimonials ("the gown was ready two days early") over vague praise.
Keep a folder of approved testimonials for your status, catalogue and capstone portfolio.

blocks.title: Show, do not boast
blocks.text: Instead of posting "We are the best!", show evidence: before-and-after photos, a short video of your packing process, a customer's permitted comment, your delivery promise kept. Evidence communicates value far better than claims.

takeaways: A value statement says who you serve, what you offer and why you are different, and must be true
Ask for referrals right after a customer shows satisfaction, with a specific, easy request
Thank referrers modestly; avoid recruitment-based schemes
Always get permission for testimonials and use customers' real words

activity.title: Build your referral kit
steps: Write your value statement using the who, what, different table.
Write a short forwardable message with your value statement and how to order.
Decide on a modest referral thank-you and write it down.
Ask at least two happy customers for a testimonial, with permission to share.
activity.evidence: Your value statement, forwardable message and at least one approved testimonial (contact details hidden)

lessons.title: Your 90-day customer plan and next steps
objectives: Choose one relationship habit and one sales skill to build over 90 days
Set measurable targets using your customer list
Assemble your capstone portfolio
Plan how you will keep learning after the course

blocks.text: Knowing what to do and doing it every week are different things. This last lesson helps you turn the course into a practical 90-day plan, and pulls together the evidence for your capstone and certificate. Keep the plan small enough to actually follow. One habit kept for 90 days changes a business more than ten ideas abandoned after a week.

blocks.name: idea-to-plan
blocks.alt: A person turning an idea into a written plan
blocks.caption: A small, written 90-day plan turns course learning into daily practice.

blocks.text: Choose your focus

Look back at your weekly service checks, complaints log and customer list. Where are you weakest? Choose **one relationship habit** (for example: follow up within two days of every delivery) and **one sales skill** (for example: always ask three open questions before recommending). Write them down.

blocks.title: Choosing what to work on first
items: Quick win: start now
Big win: plan it
Low value: skip
Costly: leave for later
blocks.caption: Start with high-impact habits that take little effort, such as follow-up messages.

blocks.text: Write each one as a clear daily or weekly action. "Follow up more" is too vague to keep. "Every evening at 6pm, send a satisfaction check to everyone who received an order in the last two days" is specific enough that you know whether you did it. Attach the habit to something you already do every day, such as closing the shop or eating dinner, so it is easier to remember.
Set measurable targets
Use the measures from Module 3 to set targets you can check. Base them on your own starting numbers, not on what other businesses do.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Grace, the skincare seller in Abuja, reviews her records. In the last month she had 25 customers, 12 of them repeat customers, she followed up with about 75% of customers after delivery, and she received 2 referrals.
steps: Relationship habit: follow up with every customer within 2 days of delivery, using a daily 6pm phone reminder.
Sales skill: ask three open questions before recommending, practised on every new enquiry.
Targets for day 90: follow-up rate from about 75% to 100%; repeat customers from 12 of 25 to at least 15 of 25; referrals from 2 to 5 a month.
Monthly check: on the last Saturday of each month, count follow-ups, repeat customers and referrals from her Google Sheet.
Support: she asks a friend in her cooperative to check in with her each month on progress.
blocks.result: Grace has a clear habit, a skill, numbers to track and a date to check them. At day 90 she will know exactly what changed.

blocks.text: When things do not go to plan

Some weeks you will miss your habit, perhaps because of illness, travel, family duties or a busy market day. That is normal. Do not abandon the plan; restart the next day. At each monthly check, ask three questions: What did I do? What changed in my numbers? What will I adjust next month? If a target was too ambitious, adjust it honestly. If a habit clearly works, keep it and consider adding a second one in your next 90 days.
Your capstone portfolio
Your capstone shows you can apply the course with real customers. Collect the following in one folder or notebook section:

items: Two or three documented customer interactions, each showing the need you discovered, how you ran the sales conversation, the outcome and your reflection.
Evidence of follow-up beyond the sale: a satisfaction check, reorder reminder or complaint resolved with LAST, with contact details hidden.
Your trust and service toolkit: terms message, payment check, five service standards.
Your customer list (numbers hidden) with your monthly measures.
Your 90-day plan with one habit, one skill, targets and check dates.

blocks.title: Privacy in your portfolio
blocks.text: Before you upload or share any screenshot, hide phone numbers, addresses and payment details. Use first names or codes such as Customer A. Only include a customer's words or photos if she has agreed.
Keep learning

items: Re-read your complaints log every month; it is your best teacher.
Watch how sellers you admire greet, follow up and handle problems, and adapt what works.
Join a cooperative, market association or women's business group to share experiences.
Continue to related WODDI Institute courses on bookkeeping, pricing or digital marketing to strengthen the rest of your business.
Revisit your 90-day plan at the end and set the next one.

blocks.text: Customer relations is a lifelong craft. The methods in this course, listening first, keeping promises, recovering well from mistakes, staying in touch and selling honestly, work for a roadside stall and a large company alike. Practise them with every customer, and they will become simply the way you do business.

takeaways: Choose one relationship habit and one sales skill for the next 90 days
Set targets from your own starting numbers and check them monthly
Your capstone portfolio shows real interactions, follow-up, your toolkit, your list and your plan
Protect customer privacy in everything you share

activity.title: Write your 90-day plan
steps: Record your starting numbers: customers, repeat customers, follow-up rate and referrals for the last month.
Choose one relationship habit and one sales skill.
Set three targets for day 90 and write your monthly check dates in your calendar.
Gather your capstone items into one folder and check each against the list.
